warmup.q: fun takeFlour(grams: Int): Int throws NotEnoughFlourException when the jar runs short. A new screen in the recipe app calls it and catches nothing. What happens on a day the jar is short?
options: The build fails until the caller handles the exception
The exception flies up through every caller until something catches it, often a general handler that shows "Something went wrong"
Kotlin wraps the exception in a Result for the caller
warmup.why: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so nothing in the signature or the build tells the caller that a short jar is possible. The exception travels up until something catches it, usually a general handler that shows an error screen. In Java, a checked throws NotEnoughFlourException would have forced a catch. This lesson puts that information back, in the return type.

opening:
Picture a recipe step that goes wrong. The custard splits. A calm cook hands back a note: "the custard split, let's serve the cake with cream instead", and dinner goes on. An upset cook throws the pan across the room, and someone further away has to catch it, or the whole dinner stops.

Code does both. An exception is the thrown pan: an object a function throws to say something failed, which flies up through every caller until some code catches it. A returned value is the note: the caller holds it and must read it. The easy trap is to throw the pan for failures that happen every week, like a jar that's out of flour, because nothing in a Kotlin signature says what might fly out.

The last lesson used null for "nothing here". Null can't say why.

In this lesson, we'll put expected failures into the return type with a sealed result, write a small result type of our own, see what kotlin.Result is for and what it swallows, and use Arrow's Either to stop at the first error or collect every one. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a custard that split and two cooks, one who hands back a note and one who throws the pan. Expected failures became notes: a sealed result the compiler checks, a railway where a note skips to the end of the line, and Arrow's either { }, which stops at the first error or, with zipOrAccumulate, collects them all. runCatching stayed at the edge, with cancellation let through.

Search your code for catch (e: Exception) and runCatching. Is each one catching a bug, an expected failure, or a cancel it should let go?

Next, we'll finish the track with data that never changes. What do val and a read-only List really promise?

sections.h: Exceptions hide the failures your caller has to handle
sections.html:
Here's the recipe app's helper that takes flour from the jar, in both languages:

Java
int takeFlour(int grams) throws NotEnoughFlourException, PastBestBeforeException;
Kotlin
fun takeFlour(grams: Int): Int   // throws NotEnoughFlourException, PastBestBeforeException

Java has checked exceptions: exceptions a method must list in its signature, so the compiler makes every caller deal with them. Kotlin has none. In the words of its docs, "Kotlin treats all exceptions as unchecked by default." So the Kotlin signature says only Int, and nothing tells the caller that the jar runs short every few weeks. A new screen forgets the try. The exception flies up past every caller, and the cook sees "Something went wrong" because the flour ran out.

The real problem is that two kinds of failure share one mechanism. An empty jar, an old bag or an amount of -5 is expected: it happens in normal use, and the caller must decide what to do. A null pointer, a broken rule inside our own code or a full disk is a bug or a broken machine, and no caller can do anything useful about it on the spot. The Kotlin team draws the same line. The design notes for kotlin.Result say: "Use nullable types or domain-specific classes to represent failures that need specific handling." The newer rich-errors proposal, KEEP-0441, says exceptions "should be used for unrecoverable cases."

So put the expected failures in the return type, as values:

Java
sealed interface TakeResult {}
record Taken(int leftGrams) implements TakeResult {}
record Refused(JarFailure reason) implements TakeResult {}
TakeResult takeFlour(int grams, int leftGrams, LocalDate bestBefore, LocalDate today);
Kotlin
sealed interface TakeResult {
    data class Taken(val leftGrams: Int) : TakeResult
    data class Refused(val reason: JarFailure) : TakeResult
}
fun takeFlour(grams: Int, leftGrams: Int, bestBefore: LocalDate, today: LocalDate): TakeResult

The jar's contents and today's date are parameters now, as the first lesson of this track taught: a pure function takes its inputs as arguments. And sealed means the compiler knows every subtype, so a when over them needs no else.

That pays off when someone adds a case. Add JarMissing to JarFailure, and every when that doesn't handle it stops compiling: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'JarMissing' branch or an 'else' branch. Java 21's sealed interfaces and pattern switch give the same check: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. That error is the whole point.

A sealed result lists every expected failure, and the compiler checks each when. Never add else to a when over a sealed type.

Exceptions keep their job for bugs. require, check and error() still belong wherever one of your own rules breaks.

A sealed type for one step works well. Chain three of them, and every step needs a when to look at the step before.

try.title: Add a failure and let the compiler find the gaps
steps: Run Exhaustive.kt. Four attempts to take flour come out as four lines of advice.
Uncomment JarMissing in JarFailure and run it again. Read the error and note which when it points at.
Add a branch for it to advice ("look in the other cupboard" will do) and run again.
Do the same in ExhaustiveJava.java.

code.title: Exhaustive.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l07.demo import java.time.LocalDate /** The expected ways taking flour from the jar can fail. A closed set: the compiler knows every case. */ sealed interface JarFailure { data class InvalidAmount(val grams: Int) : JarFailure data object PastBestBefore : JarFailure data class NotEnough(val shortByGrams: Int) : JarFailure // Uncomment the next line and run again. // data object JarMissing : JarFailure } sealed interface TakeResult { data class Taken(val leftGrams: Int) : TakeResult data class Refused(val reason: JarFailure) : TakeResult } /** The signature now says it can fail, and how. Nothing is thrown for a short jar. */ fun takeFlour(grams: Int, leftGrams: Int, bestBefore: LocalDate, today: LocalDate): TakeResult = when { grams <= 0 -> TakeResult.Refused(JarFailure.InvalidAmount(grams)) today.isAfter(bestBefore) -> TakeResult.Refused(JarFailure.PastBestBefore) grams > leftGrams -> TakeResult.Refused(JarFailure.NotEnough(grams - leftGrams)) else -> TakeResult.Taken(leftGrams - grams) } /** The one place that knows what to tell the cook: an exhaustive when with no else branch. */ fun advice(failure: JarFailure): String = when (failure) { is JarFailure.InvalidAmount -> "check the amount" JarFailure.PastBestBefore -> "open a new bag" is JarFailure.NotEnough -> "buy more flour" } fun main() { val today = LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 10) val fresh = LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 31) val old = LocalDate.of(2026, 2, 28) val attempts = listOf(200 to fresh, -5 to fresh, 200 to old, 1_000 to fresh) for ((grams, bestBefore) in attempts) { val line = when (val result = takeFlour(grams, leftGrams = 700, bestBefore, today)) { is TakeResult.Taken -> "ok: ${result.leftGrams} g left" is TakeResult.Refused -> "${advice(result.reason)}: ${result.reason}" } println(line) } }

alt.title: ExhaustiveJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l07.demo; import java.time.LocalDate; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** The same closed set of failures with Java 21 sealed interfaces, records and an exhaustive switch. */ public class ExhaustiveJava { sealed interface JarFailure {} record InvalidAmount(int grams) implements JarFailure {} record PastBestBefore() implements JarFailure {} record NotEnough(int shortByGrams) implements JarFailure {} // Uncomment the next line and run again. // record JarMissing() implements JarFailure {} sealed interface TakeResult {} record Taken(int leftGrams) implements TakeResult {} record Refused(JarFailure reason) implements TakeResult {} static TakeResult takeFlour(int grams, int leftGrams, LocalDate bestBefore, LocalDate today) { if (grams <= 0) return new Refused(new InvalidAmount(grams)); if (today.isAfter(bestBefore)) return new Refused(new PastBestBefore()); if (grams > leftGrams) return new Refused(new NotEnough(grams - leftGrams)); return new Taken(leftGrams - grams); } /** The one place that knows what to tell the cook: an exhaustive switch with no default branch. */ static String advice(JarFailure failure) { return switch (failure) { case InvalidAmount a -> "check the amount"; case PastBestBefore p -> "open a new bag"; case NotEnough n -> "buy more flour"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { LocalDate today = LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 10); LocalDate fresh = LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 31); LocalDate old = LocalDate.of(2026, 2, 28); List<Map.Entry<Integer, LocalDate>> attempts = List.of(Map.entry(200, fresh), Map.entry(-5, fresh), Map.entry(200, old), Map.entry(1_000, fresh)); for (var a : attempts) { String line = switch (takeFlour(a.getKey(), 700, a.getValue(), today)) { case Taken t -> "ok: " + t.leftGrams() + " g left"; case Refused r -> advice(r.reason()) + ": " + r.reason(); }; System.out.println(line); } } }

try.expect: The first run prints ok: 500 g left, check the amount: InvalidAmount(grams=-5), open a new bag: PastBestBefore and buy more flour: NotEnough(shortByGrams=300). With the new case, Kotlin stops at advice with 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'JarMissing' branch or an 'else' branch. The when in main still compiles, because it only looks at TakeResult. javac reports the switch expression does not cover all possible input values at the same spot. After you add the branch, both run again.

sections.h: A result type you can write in ten lines
sections.html:
One generic type can cover every step. It holds either a success with a value or a failure with an error:

Java
sealed interface Outcome<E, A> {
    default <B> Outcome<E, B> andThen(Function<? super A, Outcome<E, B>> f) {
        return switch (this) {
            case Ok<E, A> ok -> f.apply(ok.value());
            case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error());
        };
    }
}
record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {}
record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {}
Kotlin
sealed interface Outcome<out E, out A> {
    data class Ok<A>(val value: A) : Outcome<Nothing, A>
    data class Err<E>(val error: E) : Outcome<E, Nothing>
}

inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.andThen(f: (A) -> Outcome<E, B>): Outcome<E, B> =
    when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> f(value); is Outcome.Err -> this }

andThen runs the next step only if this one succeeded. An Err skips every later step and comes out at the end unchanged. Its sibling map, in the Try it, does the same for a plain function that can't fail, such as uppercase(). Making a loaf becomes one line: checkBatter(b).andThen(::mix).andThen(::bake).map { it.uppercase() }.

Picture the kitchen line from the sequences lesson, with a side door. A good batter walks down the line, step by step. When a step fails, the batter leaves through the side door with a note pinned to it, and the note walks straight to the end of the line, past every step still waiting. Programmers draw the same idea as a railway with two tracks, success on top and failure below, which is why the style is called railway-oriented programming. The figure shows it.

Look at the variance. Outcome<out E, out A> is covariant in both parameters: an Outcome of a subtype counts as an Outcome of its supertype ("Covariance with out: producers" in the generics track). And Err is an Outcome<E, Nothing>. Nothing is the type with no values at all, and it's a subtype of every type. So an Err<BakeErr> already is an Outcome<BakeErr, String>, an Outcome<BakeErr, Loaf>, an Outcome<BakeErr, X> for any X. That's why is Outcome.Err -> this compiles without building a new object. Java has no declaration-site variance (variance written once, on the type itself) and no Nothing, so the Java version builds a new Err at every step.

The kitchen picture breaks at one point. A cook who gets a note can still decide to carry on with a second-best dish; this line never does. Once a value is an Err, nothing after it runs, unless you write a step that looks for errors on purpose. Arrow, later in this lesson, calls that step recover.

That's all an Either is at heart: a value that holds one of two things, an error or a result. Libraries add more helpers, and a block syntax that makes chains read like straight-line code. Before we get there, the standard library ships one result type of its own, and it was built for a different job.

Once on the failure track, the note travels to the end and no later step runs."><text class="t-s t-ok" x="20" y="84">success</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="20" y="194">failure</text><line class="ln-a" x1="80" y1="80" x2="600" y2="80" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-bad" x1="80" y1="190" x2="600" y2="190" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box" x="115" y="60" width="110" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="170" y="85" text-anchor="middle">check</text><rect class="box" x="275" y="60" width="110" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="330" y="85" text-anchor="middle">mix</text><rect class="box" x="435" y="60" width="110" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="490" y="85" text-anchor="middle">bake</text><line class="ln-bad" x1="200" y1="100" x2="250" y2="186" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-bad" x1="360" y1="100" x2="410" y2="186" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-bad" x1="520" y1="100" x2="570" y2="186" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-bad" x="250" y="146" text-anchor="middle">Invalid</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="412" y="146" text-anchor="middle">BowlTooSmall</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="574" y="146" text-anchor="middle">Burnt</text><text class="t-s t-ok" x="560" y="56" text-anchor="middle">Ok(loaf)</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="520" y="214" text-anchor="middle">Err(the first note)</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="320" y="248" text-anchor="middle">andThen runs a step only on the success track; map changes the value there</text></svg>

try.title: Walk a batter down the line
steps: Read Outcome.kt. Each step prints its name when it runs. For each of the three batters, predict which names print and what comes out.
Run it, then run OutcomeJava.java.
In Outcome.kt, change is Outcome.Err -> this in map to is Outcome.Err -> Outcome.Err(error). Does it still compile? Why was this allowed?

code.title: Outcome.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l07.demo /** A hand-written result type: a success holding a value, or a failure holding an error. */ sealed interface Outcome<out E, out A> { data class Ok<A>(val value: A) : Outcome<Nothing, A> data class Err<E>(val error: E) : Outcome<E, Nothing> } /** Change the value on the success track; a failure passes through untouched. */ inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.map(f: (A) -> B): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> Outcome.Ok(f(value)); is Outcome.Err -> this } /** Run the next step that can fail, only on the success track. */ inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.andThen(f: (A) -> Outcome<E, B>): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> f(value); is Outcome.Err -> this } sealed interface BakeErr { data class Invalid(val why: String) : BakeErr data object BowlTooSmall : BakeErr } data class Batter(val flourGrams: Int) fun checkBatter(b: Batter): Outcome<BakeErr, Batter> { println(" check") return if (b.flourGrams > 0) Outcome.Ok(b) else Outcome.Err(BakeErr.Invalid("flour<=0")) } fun mix(b: Batter): Outcome<BakeErr, String> { println(" mix") return if (b.flourGrams <= 1_000) Outcome.Ok("dough") else Outcome.Err(BakeErr.BowlTooSmall) } fun bake(dough: String): Outcome<BakeErr, String> { println(" bake") return Outcome.Ok("loaf from $dough") } fun makeLoaf(b: Batter) = checkBatter(b).andThen(::mix).andThen(::bake).map { it.uppercase() } fun main() { for (b in listOf(Batter(500), Batter(-1), Batter(5_000))) { println("$b:") println(" -> ${makeLoaf(b)}") } }

alt.title: OutcomeJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l07.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Function; /** The same result type in Java 21. Without declaration-site variance and Nothing, Err must be rebuilt each step. */ public class OutcomeJava { sealed interface Outcome<E, A> { default <B> Outcome<E, B> map(Function<? super A, ? extends B> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> new Ok<>(f.apply(ok.value())); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); // a new Err with a new type }; } default <B> Outcome<E, B> andThen(Function<? super A, Outcome<E, B>> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> f.apply(ok.value()); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); }; } } record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {} record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {} sealed interface BakeErr {} record Invalid(String why) implements BakeErr {} record BowlTooSmall() implements BakeErr {} record Batter(int flourGrams) {} static Outcome<BakeErr, Batter> check(Batter b) { System.out.println(" check"); return b.flourGrams() > 0 ? new Ok<>(b) : new Err<>(new Invalid("flour<=0")); } static Outcome<BakeErr, String> mix(Batter b) { System.out.println(" mix"); return b.flourGrams() <= 1_000 ? new Ok<>("dough") : new Err<>(new BowlTooSmall()); } static Outcome<BakeErr, String> bake(String dough) { System.out.println(" bake"); return new Ok<>("loaf from " + dough); } static Outcome<BakeErr, String> makeLoaf(Batter b) { return check(b).andThen(OutcomeJava::mix).andThen(OutcomeJava::bake).map(String::toUpperCase); } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Batter b : List.of(new Batter(500), new Batter(-1), new Batter(5_000))) { System.out.println(b + ":"); System.out.println(" -> " + makeLoaf(b)); } } }

try.expect: Batter(flourGrams=500) runs all three steps and gives Ok(value=LOAF FROM DOUGH). Batter(flourGrams=-1) prints only check and gives Err(error=Invalid(why=flour<=0)). Batter(flourGrams=5000) prints check and mix and gives Err(error=BowlTooSmall): bake never runs. Java prints the same steps. Both versions of the Err branch compile; this works because an Outcome<E, Nothing> is already an Outcome<E, B> for every B, so there's no need to build a new object.

sections.h: kotlin.Result wraps code that throws, and swallows cancellation
sections.html:
The standard library has one result type, kotlin.Result<T>, and runCatching { } makes one: it runs the block and catches whatever the block throws. Result isn't an Either. It has a single type parameter, and the failure is always a Throwable, the parent class of every exception and error on the JVM. Its design notes are blunt: "The Result class is not designed to represent domain-specific error conditions." It was built mainly for the coroutine machinery: Continuation.resumeWith takes a Result.

Use it at the edge, around code that throws when you'd rather have a value. Here the app reads a recipe file that a user imported, and falls back to an empty recipe when the file is broken:

Java
Recipe recipe;
try { recipe = importer.parse(file); }      // a Java library that throws
catch (Exception e) { recipe = Recipe.EMPTY; }
Kotlin
val recipe = runCatching { importer.parse(file) }   // a Java library that throws
    .getOrElse { Recipe.EMPTY }

Two traps come with it. The first is that runCatching catches every Throwable. It catches everything you throw at it, including the message that tells it to stop. That covers OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError, and inside a coroutine it covers CancellationException, the exception that carries a cancel.

A coroutine is a light task that can pause while it waits, without holding on to a thread, and you cancel one to say "stop, nobody wants the answer any more" ("Cancellation and timeouts" in the coroutines track). The Try it cancels a coroutine while it waits for the shop inside runCatching. The cancel turns into a failed Result. The coroutine runs on until its next suspension point, the next place where it could pause, and the line that places the order runs. An issue asking kotlinx.coroutines for a runCatching that rethrows CancellationException (#1814) has been open since February 2020. Until something ships, rethrow it yourself, as the lab asks:

Java
// Java equivalent: never swallow the interrupt that carries a stop request
try { return shop.ask(item); }
catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new CancellationException(); }
Kotlin
runCatching { shop.ask(item) }                               // a suspend call that waits for the shop
    .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }   // a cancel keeps travelling

The second trap is that map doesn't catch. runCatching { "12".toInt() }.map { error("boom") } throws IllegalStateException: boom straight out of map. Only mapCatching turns it into Failure(java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom). The library pairs recover and recoverCatching the same way. If a chain should be safe from end to end, every step that can throw needs the Catching variant.

So Result answers one question: did this throwing call work? It can't say which kitchen failure happened. fun order(item: Ingredient): Result<Delivery> tells the caller less than the sealed type from the first section.

Keep runCatching at the edge, around code that throws. Let CancellationException through.

For our own failures we want the railway back, with a nicer shape. That's Arrow's Either, and it brings a second mode the railway never had.

try.title: Cancel an order inside runCatching
steps: Read part 1 of RunCatchingTrap.kt. The coroutine is cancelled after 50 ms, while it waits for the shop inside runCatching. Predict: does placing the order anyway print, and what's in orders?
Run it and compare part 1 with part 2.
Read part 3 and predict which line throws.
Run RunCatchingTrapJava.java, which makes the same mistake with a thread and catch (Exception e).

code.title: RunCatchingTrap.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l07.demo import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException fun main() = runBlocking<Unit> { println("1. runCatching around a suspend call, cancelled after 50 ms:") val placed = mutableListOf<String>() val swallowing = launch { val r = runCatching { delay(1_000); "basket-1" } // waiting for the shop to answer println(" runCatching returned: isFailure=${r.isFailure} ex=${r.exceptionOrNull()?.javaClass?.simpleName}") println(" isActive after swallow = $isActive") placed += "placed the order" println(" placing the order anyway (code with no suspension point keeps running)") try { delay(1) } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" next suspension point throws: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") throw e } } delay(50) swallowing.cancelAndJoin() println(" orders: $placed") println("2. the same, with CancellationException rethrown:") val placed2 = mutableListOf<String>() val rethrowing = launch { val r = runCatching { delay(1_000); "basket-1" }.onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it } placed2 += "placed the order ($r)" } delay(50) rethrowing.cancelAndJoin() println(" cancelled=${rethrowing.isCancelled}, orders: $placed2") println("3. map rethrows, mapCatching captures:") val parsed = runCatching { "12".toInt() } println(" mapCatching: ${parsed.mapCatching { error("boom") }}") try { parsed.map { error("boom") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println(" map threw: IllegalStateException: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: RunCatchingTrapJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l07.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; /** * Java equivalent of RunCatchingTrap.kt: a catch-everything block around a blocking call swallows the * interrupt, the thread's stop signal, and the code after it places the order anyway. */ public class RunCatchingTrapJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("1. catch (Exception e) around sleep, interrupted after 50 ms:"); List<String> placed = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Thread swallowing = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(1_000); // waiting for the shop } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" caught " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", carrying on"); } placed.add("placed the order"); }); swallowing.start(); Thread.sleep(50); swallowing.interrupt(); swallowing.join(); System.out.println(" orders: " + placed); System.out.println("2. the same, with the interrupt restored and the work stopped:"); List<String> placed2 = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Thread stopping = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(1_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the signal return; // and stop } placed2.add("placed the order"); }); stopping.start(); Thread.sleep(50); stopping.interrupt(); stopping.join(); System.out.println(" orders: " + placed2); } }

try.expect: Part 1 prints runCatching returned: isFailure=true ex=JobCancellationException, isActive after swallow = false, then placing the order anyway, and only the next delay throws. orders holds placed the order: work ran after the cancel. Part 2 rethrows, so the job ends cancelled=true with no orders. In part 3, mapCatching returns Failure(java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom) and map throws. Java's thread catches InterruptedException, carries on and places the order; restoring the interrupt flag and returning fixes it.

sections.h: Arrow's Either: stop at the first error, or collect every one
sections.html:
Arrow is a functional programming library for Kotlin, and the lab uses arrow-core 2.3.0. Its Either<E, A> is the Outcome from earlier, Left(error) or Right(value), plus an either { } block that replaces chains of andThen. Here's the lab's grocery order: reserve the ingredient at the shop, check that the delivery arrives in time, then book it:

Java
// Java equivalent: the hand-written Outcome from earlier, chained with andThen
Outcome<KitchenError, Delivery> order(Ingredient ingredient, Shop shop) {
    return shop.reserve(ingredient).andThen(basketId -> {
        int minutes = shop.deliveryMinutes(basketId);
        if (minutes >= LATEST_MINUTES) return new Err<>(new TooLate(minutes));
        return shop.book(basketId).map(slotId -> new Delivery(basketId, slotId));
    });
}
Kotlin
fun order(ingredient: Ingredient, shop: Shop): Either<KitchenError, Delivery> = either {
    val basketId = shop.reserve(ingredient).bind()          // a Left ends the block here
    val minutes = shop.deliveryMinutes(basketId)
    ensure(minutes < LATEST_MINUTES) { KitchenError.TooLate(minutes) }
    val slotId = shop.book(basketId).bind()
    Delivery(basketId, slotId)
}

Inside either { }, .bind() unwraps a Right. On a Left it stops the block, and that Left becomes the result. ensure(condition) { error } stops the block when the condition is false. The code reads top to bottom like the happy path, and it is fail-fast: the first failure wins, and nothing after it runs.

Fail-fast is right for a line of steps where each needs the one before. It's wrong for a form. A cook who types an amount of -5 with the unit oz (the scale was left on ounces again) should hear about both at once, not one per try. zipOrAccumulate runs independent checks, collects every failure into a NonEmptyList, a list that always holds at least one item, and calls its last lambda only if all of them passed:

Java
// Java equivalent: run every check and collect the errors by hand
Validated<Amount> accumulate(int a, String u) {
    List<FormError> errors = new ArrayList<>();
    if (a <= 0) errors.add(new InvalidAmount(a));
    if (!UNITS.contains(u)) errors.add(new UnsupportedUnit(u));
    return errors.isEmpty() ? new Valid<>(new Amount(a, u)) : new Invalid<>(List.copyOf(errors));
}
Kotlin
fun accumulate(a: Int, u: String): Either<NonEmptyList<FormError>, Amount> = either {
    zipOrAccumulate({ validAmount(a) }, { validUnit(u) }) { amount, unit -> Amount(amount, unit) }
}
// accumulate(-5, "oz") is Either.Left([InvalidAmount(amount=-5), UnsupportedUnit(unit=oz)])

validAmount and validUnit are functions with a Raise<FormError> receiver, so the ensure inside them can stop whichever block called them. The same input through a plain either { Amount(validAmount(-5), validUnit("oz")) } gives only Either.Left(InvalidAmount(amount=-5)).

Stop at the first error when each step needs the one before. Collect every error when the checks don't depend on each other.

For code that throws, Either.catch { } is the safer cousin of runCatching. It turns an ordinary exception into a Left, but it rethrows CancellationException and fatal errors such as OutOfMemoryError.

You may have read that Kotlin is getting error unions, fun load(): Recipe | NotFound. That's a real proposal (KEEP-0441, with the detailed design in KEEP-0462), but it isn't in Kotlin 2.4.21: the compiler rejects error class NotFound with Syntax error: Expecting a top level declaration. Today the picker is short. Use a nullable type when absence needs no reason. Use a sealed type for a few outcomes of one function. Use Either when many steps chain or errors must be collected. Keep Result for code that throws, and exceptions for bugs.

try.title: Fail fast, then collect everything
steps: Read EitherDemo.kt. Predict what failFast(-5, "oz") and accumulate(-5, "oz") print.
Run it.
Change accumulate(-5, "oz") to accumulate(250, "oz"). Predict the result, then run it.
Run EitherDemoJava.java and compare how much code the Java version needs per rule.

code.title: EitherDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l07.demo import arrow.core.Either import arrow.core.NonEmptyList import arrow.core.raise.Raise import arrow.core.raise.either import arrow.core.raise.ensure import arrow.core.raise.zipOrAccumulate import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException sealed interface FormError { data class InvalidAmount(val amount: Int) : FormError data class UnsupportedUnit(val unit: String) : FormError } data class Amount(val amount: Int, val unit: String) fun Raise<FormError>.validAmount(a: Int): Int { ensure(a > 0) { FormError.InvalidAmount(a) } return a } fun Raise<FormError>.validUnit(u: String): String { ensure(u in setOf("g", "ml", "pcs")) { FormError.UnsupportedUnit(u) } return u } /** Stops at the first failure: the second check never runs. */ fun failFast(a: Int, u: String): Either<FormError, Amount> = either { Amount(validAmount(a), validUnit(u)) } /** Runs every check and collects every failure. */ fun accumulate(a: Int, u: String): Either<NonEmptyList<FormError>, Amount> = either { zipOrAccumulate({ validAmount(a) }, { validUnit(u) }) { amount, unit -> Amount(amount, unit) } } fun main() { println("fail fast: ${failFast(-5, "oz")}") println("accumulate: ${accumulate(-5, "oz")}") println("all good: ${accumulate(250, "g")}") println("Either.catch around code that throws:") println(" ${Either.catch { "2OO".toInt() }.mapLeft { it::class.simpleName }}") // the letter O, twice try { Either.catch { throw CancellationException("shopping cancelled") } } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" CancellationException rethrown, not captured") } }

alt.title: EitherDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l07.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** Java equivalent: the JDK has no Either. A small sealed result and a list of errors do both jobs by hand. */ public class EitherDemoJava { sealed interface FormError {} record InvalidAmount(int amount) implements FormError {} record UnsupportedUnit(String unit) implements FormError {} record Amount(int amount, String unit) {} sealed interface Validated<A> {} record Valid<A>(A value) implements Validated<A> {} record Invalid<A>(List<FormError> errors) implements Validated<A> {} static final Set<String> UNITS = Set.of("g", "ml", "pcs"); /** Stops at the first failure: the second check never runs. */ static Validated<Amount> failFast(int a, String u) { if (a <= 0) return new Invalid<>(List.of(new InvalidAmount(a))); if (!UNITS.contains(u)) return new Invalid<>(List.of(new UnsupportedUnit(u))); return new Valid<>(new Amount(a, u)); } /** Runs every check and collects every failure. */ static Validated<Amount> accumulate(int a, String u) { List<FormError> errors = new ArrayList<>(); if (a <= 0) errors.add(new InvalidAmount(a)); if (!UNITS.contains(u)) errors.add(new UnsupportedUnit(u)); return errors.isEmpty() ? new Valid<>(new Amount(a, u)) : new Invalid<>(List.copyOf(errors)); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("fail fast: " + failFast(-5, "oz")); System.out.println("accumulate: " + accumulate(-5, "oz")); System.out.println("all good: " + accumulate(250, "g")); } }

try.expect: fail fast: Either.Left(InvalidAmount(amount=-5)): the unit check never ran. accumulate: Either.Left([InvalidAmount(amount=-5), UnsupportedUnit(unit=oz)]). With a good amount, only Either.Left([UnsupportedUnit(unit=oz)]) remains: still a list, now with one item. Either.catch turns "2OO".toInt(), typed with two letter Os, into Either.Left(NumberFormatException) and lets the CancellationException through. Java prints the same results with a hand-built list.

compare.title: A fail-fast grocery order: Java sealed result vs Kotlin either { }

java.title: Order.java
java.html: sealed interface Outcome<E, A> { /* map and andThen as in section 2 */ } record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {} record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {} Outcome<KitchenError, Delivery> order(Ingredient ingredient, Shop shop) { return shop.reserve(ingredient).andThen(basketId -> { // 1. reserve int minutes = shop.deliveryMinutes(basketId); // 2. check the time if (minutes >= LATEST_MINUTES) return new Err<>(new TooLate(minutes)); return shop.book(basketId) // 3. book .map(slotId -> new Delivery(basketId, slotId)); }); }

kotlin.title: Order.kt
kotlin.html: fun order(ingredient: Ingredient, shop: Shop): Either<KitchenError, Delivery> = either { val basketId = shop.reserve(ingredient).bind() // 1. reserve val minutes = shop.deliveryMinutes(basketId) // 2. check the time ensure(minutes < LATEST_MINUTES) { KitchenError.TooLate(minutes) } val slotId = shop.book(basketId).bind() // 3. book Delivery(basketId, slotId) }

compare.note: Both are the same railway: the first Err or Left ends the pipeline and comes back unchanged, and the sealed error type keeps every when or switch over it exhaustive. The differences are in how it reads and what the library brings. Java nests a lambda per step, so a five-step pipeline drifts to the right, and every Err has to be rebuilt because Java has no Nothing and no declaration-site variance. Kotlin's either { } keeps the steps flat: bind() and ensure stop the block with the error, so the code reads like the happy path. Arrow also brings what the hand-written version lacks: zipOrAccumulate and mapOrAccumulate for collecting errors, Either.catch that lets cancellation through, and mapLeft and recover for translating errors between layers.

worked.title: Layer the "order it" button: check everything, then stop at the first failure

steps.say: The cook types an ingredient line and taps "order it". 1. Check the line at the edge and collect every problem, so the cook fixes the whole line at once. The lab's validate returns Either<NonEmptyList<KitchenError>, Ingredient>.
steps.code: val checked: Either<NonEmptyList<KitchenError>, Ingredient> = validate(form) // IngredientForm("fl0ur", -5, "oz", "") gives Left([InvalidName(name=fl0ur), InvalidAmount(amount=-5), UnsupportedUnit(unit=oz)])

alt.html: Validated<Ingredient> checked = validate(form); // every rule runs; the errors are collected if (checked instanceof Invalid<Ingredient> invalid) return showProblems(invalid.errors());

steps.say: 1. Run the shop steps fail-fast, and give the two kinds of error one type so the button can show either. mapLeft changes the error side and leaves a Right alone.
steps.code: sealed interface ScreenError { data class Invalid(val errors: NonEmptyList<KitchenError>) : ScreenError data class Failed(val error: KitchenError) : ScreenError } fun orderIt(form: IngredientForm, shop: Shop): Either<ScreenError, Delivery> = either { val ingredient = validate(form).mapLeft(ScreenError::Invalid).bind() // every line error at once order(ingredient, shop).mapLeft(ScreenError::Failed).bind() // the first shop failure }

alt.html: sealed interface ScreenError {} record InvalidLine(List<KitchenError> errors) implements ScreenError {} record Failed(KitchenError error) implements ScreenError {} Outcome<ScreenError, Delivery> orderIt(IngredientForm form, Shop shop) { return switch (validate(form)) { case Invalid<Ingredient> invalid -> new Err<>(new InvalidLine(invalid.errors())); // every line error case Valid<Ingredient> valid -> switch (order(valid.value(), shop)) { // the first shop failure case Ok<KitchenError, Delivery> ok -> new Ok<>(ok.value()); case Err<KitchenError, Delivery> err -> new Err<>(new Failed(err.error())); }; }; }

steps.say: 1. At the outer edge, the shop's own client library throws when the network gives up. Turn the one failure that means something to the cook into a value, and let everything else fly. A SocketTimeoutException (the network call gave up waiting) becomes ShopClosed, which the screen can show; an IllegalStateException is a bug and must stay an exception.
steps.code: fun ShopClient.reserveSafely(body: String): Either<KitchenError, String> = Either.catch { post(body) } // rethrows CancellationException and fatal errors .mapLeft { e -> if (e is SocketTimeoutException) KitchenError.ShopClosed else throw e }

alt.html: Outcome<KitchenError, String> reserveSafely(ShopClient client, String body) throws IOException { try { return new Ok<>(client.post(body)); } catch (SocketTimeoutException e) { return new Err<>(new ShopClosed()); // the one failure that means something to the cook } // other exceptions fly on: a bug stays a bug }

steps.say: 1. Turn errors into screen messages in exactly one place, with an exhaustive when and no else. When someone adds a KitchenError case next year, this function stops compiling until they decide what the cook should read.
steps.code: fun message(error: ScreenError): String = when (error) { is ScreenError.Invalid -> "Please fix ${error.errors.size} things in this line" is ScreenError.Failed -> when (error.error) { KitchenError.OutOfStock -> "The shop is out of it" is KitchenError.TooLate -> "It would arrive after your guests" KitchenError.ShopClosed -> "The shop isn't answering, try later" is KitchenError.InvalidName, is KitchenError.InvalidAmount, is KitchenError.UnsupportedUnit, is KitchenError.NoteTooLong -> "Please check this line" } }

alt.html: String message(ScreenError error) { return switch (error) { case InvalidLine i -> "Please fix " + i.errors().size() + " things in this line"; case Failed f -> switch (f.error()) { case OutOfStock o -> "The shop is out of it"; case TooLate t -> "It would arrive after your guests"; case ShopClosed c -> "The shop isn't answering, try later"; case InvalidName n -> "Please check this line"; case InvalidAmount a -> "Please check this line"; case UnsupportedUnit u -> "Please check this line"; case NoteTooLong l -> "Please check this line"; }; }; }

lab.title: Check a line, order it, and keep cancellation working
steps: Run the tests. Ten of twelve fail. The two that pass check runCatchingCancellable with a value and an ordinary exception, where plain runCatching already works. Model.kt holds the types and needs no changes.
In Validation.kt, write checkName and checkNote in the style of the two rules above them.
Write validate as either { zipOrAccumulate(...) { ... } }, with the four checks in the order the KDoc gives: name, amount, unit, note.
In Pipeline.kt, write order as one either { } block: bind() each shop call that returns an Either, and ensure the delivery time.

In SafeCatching.kt, make runCatchingCancellable rethrow CancellationException. The cancellation test runs on the virtual time of kotlinx-coroutines-test, a clock the test controls, so it finishes at once.
Run the tests until all twelve pass.
hints: zipOrAccumulate takes up to nine lambdas and then a final lambda that receives their results. Inside each lambda you can call the check... functions directly, because the lambdas run in a Raise context.
In order, read the minutes into a val first, then ensure(minutes < LATEST_MINUTES) { KitchenError.TooLate(minutes) }.

Import CancellationException from kotlin.coroutines.cancellation. Catch it before the general Throwable clause and rethrow it, or use runCatching { block() }.onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }.
If either or zipOrAccumulate won't resolve, add import arrow.core.raise.either and import arrow.core.raise.zipOrAccumulate.

drill.title: A railway from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Outcome<E, A> with its two cases, map and andThen, with the variance that lets an error pass through unchanged. Then chain checkBatter, mix and bake with it. Check: does your Err branch need to build a new object?

answer.html: sealed interface Outcome<out E, out A> { data class Ok<A>(val value: A) : Outcome<Nothing, A> data class Err<E>(val error: E) : Outcome<E, Nothing> } inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.map(f: (A) -> B): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> Outcome.Ok(f(value)); is Outcome.Err -> this } // Err<E> is an Outcome<E, B> inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.andThen(f: (A) -> Outcome<E, B>): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> f(value); is Outcome.Err -> this } fun makeLoaf(b: Batter) = checkBatter(b).andThen(::mix).andThen(::bake)

alt.html: sealed interface Outcome<E, A> { default <B> Outcome<E, B> map(Function<? super A, ? extends B> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> new Ok<>(f.apply(ok.value())); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); // Java must rebuild the Err }; } default <B> Outcome<E, B> andThen(Function<? super A, Outcome<E, B>> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> f.apply(ok.value()); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); }; } } record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {} record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {} Outcome<BakeErr, String> makeLoaf(Batter b) { return checkBatter(b).andThen(this::mix).andThen(this::bake); }

recap: Expected failures, such as an empty jar or a unit the app doesn't know, belong in the return type as values. Bugs and broken machines stay exceptions.
A sealed result with an exhaustive when and no else makes the compiler list every case you forgot to handle.
A two-case result with map and andThen is a railway: each step runs only on the success track. out variance and Nothing let an error pass through unchanged.
kotlin.Result wraps code that throws. runCatching catches every Throwable, CancellationException included, and map doesn't catch: use mapCatching.
Arrow's either { } with bind and ensure is fail-fast; zipOrAccumulate runs every check and collects the errors in a NonEmptyList.

The limit: a returned error only helps if someone reads it. Kotlin 2.4.21 doesn't warn about an ignored return value by default, and error unions like Recipe | NotFound are still a proposal (KEEP-0441, KEEP-0462).

explain.prompt: A teammate proposes fun order(item: Ingredient): Result<Delivery> for the app's grocery feature, "because Result is Kotlin's built-in way to return errors". Explain why it's a poor fit, and what you'd use instead.
explain.answer: Result has one type parameter, and its failure side is always a Throwable, so the signature says "this can fail somehow" and nothing about how. The caller can't tell an empty shelf from a late delivery from a shop that isn't answering without inspecting exception classes, and the compiler won't check that every case is handled. The Kotlin team's own design notes say Result isn't meant for domain errors. It also comes from runCatching, which catches CancellationException and fatal errors unless you're careful. I'd model the expected failures as a sealed KitchenError (OutOfStock, TooLate, ShopClosed, ...) and return Either<KitchenError, Delivery>, or a sealed result type if we don't want Arrow. Then a when over the error is exhaustive, adding a case breaks the build where it must be handled, and real bugs stay exceptions for the general handler.

deeper.html:
Three parts of Arrow are worth knowing once either { } feels natural.

Raise without Either. The lab's checks are functions with a Raise<KitchenError> receiver: they don't return an Either, they raise inside whatever block calls them. Kotlin 2.4.0 made context parameters Stable, and Arrow 2.3.0 ships matching versions of ensure, raise and bind in the arrow.core.raise.context package, so the same check can be written as context(_: Raise<KitchenError>) fun checkUnit(unit: String): String. With Kotlin 2.4.21 that compiles without any compiler flag. Arrow's own docs still show the extension-receiver style and describe context parameters as a future option, so expect both styles in code you read.

Collections and the experimental block. mapOrAccumulate checks every element of a list and collects the failures: running it over the amounts [10, -1, 20, -2] gives Either.Left([InvalidAmount(amount=-1), InvalidAmount(amount=-2)]). There is also an accumulate { ensureOrAccumulate(...) } block that reads like a list of checks. In Arrow 2.3.0 it is still marked @ExperimentalRaiseAccumulateApi, so you opt in with @OptIn(ExperimentalRaiseAccumulateApi::class); zipOrAccumulate is the stable choice.

Translating errors between layers. mapLeft changes the error value and leaves a Right alone, as in the worked example. recover is more general: inside it you can run any computation that may itself raise, for example trying a second shop when the first returns ShopClosed. Use mapLeft to rename errors at a boundary, and recover to handle them.
